content.intro: Learn limiting the number of results through a short explanation, a concept diagram, and a PostgreSQL-oriented example. Focus on the reason for the query or design decision before memorizing syntax.
content.why_it_matters: Limiting the Number of Results matters because database behavior becomes more reliable when the intended row meaning, data shape, and edge cases are explicit. This lesson follows the SQL curriculum's listed subtopics and calls out PostgreSQL-specific behavior when it matters.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: The practical goal of limiting the number of results is to produce a result set whose meaning is clear. Confirm which rows enter the query, how values are transformed or combined, and whether NULLs, duplicates, ties, or one-to-many relationships change the output.

content_blocks.title: Apply the idea
content_blocks.text: Start with the subtopics: LIMIT where supported, FETCH FIRST and standard-style alternatives, Dialect-specific row-limiting syntax, Combining sorting with row limits. Define the result you expect, run or inspect the small example in your own disposable PostgreSQL lab, and change one assumption at a time. The embedded lesson editor is a demonstration shell: the current project shows the sample expected output and does not execute arbitrary SQL on the server.

items.title: LIMIT where supported
items.text: LIMIT where supported helps you read and shape result sets with SELECT, expressions, aliases, sorting, filtering, limits, pagination, and careful NULL reasoning. Start with a concrete example, state the expected result, and verify the behavior before extending the query or design.

items.title: Returning the top results correctly
items.text: Returning the top results correctly changes stored data. Preview the target rows, specify a restrictive predicate where appropriate, validate constraints, and wrap related changes in a transaction that can be reviewed before commit.

content_blocks.code:
SELECT product_id, name, price
FROM products
ORDER BY price DESC, product_id
FETCH FIRST 5 ROWS ONLY;
content_blocks.expected_output: The unique product_id tie-breaker makes the top-five selection deterministic when prices tie.

content_blocks.title: Remember
content_blocks.text: SQL correctness depends on data shape, constraints, NULL behavior, row counts, and the target database dialect—not just whether a statement parses.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a query is correct because it returns some rows.
common_mistakes.why: A result can omit valid records, multiply joined rows, mishandle NULLs, or rely on a non-deterministic order.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the expected row grain, add targeted edge cases, and use a stable tie-breaker whenever order or pagination matters.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying PostgreSQL syntax into another SQL engine without checking support.
common_mistakes.why: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, SQL Server, and Oracle differ in types, functions, row limits, procedural features, and transaction behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Label the target engine/version and verify the relevant official reference before adapting the query.

common_mistakes.problem: Testing with production data or credentials.
common_mistakes.why: Practice statements can change rows or expose sensitive information if run against the wrong connection.
common_mistakes.fix: Use a dedicated disposable lab, check current_database() and current_user, and review all changes before committing.
